props.title: Diego Maradona

sections.content: Asif Kapadia's **Diego Maradona (2019)** (2019) represents the pinnacle of sports documentary filmmaking, following his masterful Senna (2010) and **Amy** (2015). Using over 500 hours of never-before-seen footage, Kapadia crafts an intimate portrait of football's most controversial genius during his time at Napoli. The film brilliantly contrasts "Diego" - the humble boy from the slums - with "Maradona" - the larger-than-life football god who succumbed to cocaine addiction and organized crime connections.

sections.content: Sports documentaries reached new heights in the 2010s, with filmmakers applying sophisticated narrative techniques to athletic subjects. **The Last Dance** (2020) revolutionized the format by weaving multiple timelines around Michael Jordan's final Bulls season. **When We Were Kings** (1996) set the template by capturing both Muhammad Ali's larger-than-life personality and the cultural significance of the "Rumble in the Jungle."

Like **Maradona**, these films transcend sports by examining how exceptional talent intersects with fame, power, and human frailty. **Icarus** (2017) began as a cycling documentary before accidentally exposing Russia's state-sponsored doping program. **Free Solo** (2018) uses Alex Honnold's death-defying climbs to explore the psychology of obsession. SUBHEAD: The Rise of Archival Documentary

movies.title: Senna
movies.slug: Masterful documentary about Formula 1 champion Ayrton Senna using entirely archival footage

sections.content: Kapadia pioneered a distinctive style that relies entirely on archival footage, avoiding talking heads and contemporary interviews. This approach creates remarkable immediacy, as seen in **Amy** (2015) and **Diego Maradona** (2019). The technique influenced later works like **Val** (2021), built from Val Kilmer's personal video archives, and **The Last Dance** (2020), which seamlessly blends 1990s footage with present-day interviews.
